\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{собака} (sobáka)}{собака (sobáka)}]{\ru{собака} (sobáka) — a dog}

\label{lesson:RU-C60-dog}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Russian for the weather, then the Russian for the world; peace.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{собака}}
\textbf{\ru{собака}} (\emph{sobáka}) — \textquotedblleft{}a dog\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{собака}} — origin disputed. Vasmer takes it from a Middle Iranian \emph{*sabāka-}, compare Median \emph{spaka}, \textquotedblleft{}dog\textquotedblright{}, which Herodotus records, a cousin of Greek \emph{kýōn}, \textquotedblleft{}dog\textquotedblright{}. Trubachev, in a note, finds an Iranian source unlikely and prefers Turkic \emph{köbäk}, \textquotedblleft{}dog\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sobáka}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Russian for the weather, then the Russian for the world; peace, then say \emph{sobáka} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{кошка} (kóshka)}{кошка (kóshka)}]{\ru{кошка} (kóshka) — a cat}

\label{lesson:RU-C60-cat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Russian for the world; peace, then the Russian for a dog.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{кошка}}
\textbf{\ru{кошка}} (\emph{kóshka}) — \textquotedblleft{}a cat\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{кошка}} — probably a fond form built on \emph{\ru{кот}}, \textquotedblleft{}a tomcat\textquotedblright{}, as the pet name \emph{\ru{Маша}} is built on \emph{\ru{Мария}}, \textquotedblleft{}Mary\textquotedblright{} (Vasmer). Old Russian had \emph{kotŭka}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{лошадь} (lóshad)}{лошадь (lóshad)}]{\ru{лошадь} (lóshad) — a horse}

\label{lesson:RU-C60-horse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Russian for a dog, then the Russian for a cat.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{лошадь}}
\textbf{\ru{лошадь}} (\emph{lóshad}) — \textquotedblleft{}a horse\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{лошадь}} — an old loan from Turkic, says Vasmer: compare Chuvash \emph{laša}, \textquotedblleft{}horse\textquotedblright{}, and Turkish and Tatar \emph{alaša}, \textquotedblleft{}a horse, a gelding\textquotedblright{}. It grew from \emph{\ru{лоша}}, with a suffix; the native word is \emph{\ru{конь}}, \textquotedblleft{}a steed\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{корова} (koróva)}{корова (koróva)}]{\ru{корова} (koróva) — a cow}

\label{lesson:RU-C60-cow}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Russian for a cat, then the Russian for a horse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{корова}}
\textbf{\ru{корова}} (\emph{koróva}) — \textquotedblleft{}a cow\textquotedblright{}. It gives \textbf{\ru{молоко}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{корова}} $\leftarrow$ Proto-Slavic \emph{*korva} — inherited, a cousin of Lithuanian \emph{kárvė}, \textquotedblleft{}cow\textquotedblright{}, and, Vasmer says, of Greek \emph{keraós}, \textquotedblleft{}horned\textquotedblright{}, and Latin \emph{cervus}, \textquotedblleft{}deer\textquotedblright{}: the horned one. Church Slavonic has \emph{\ru{крава}}, \textquotedblleft{}cow\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{свинья} (svinyá)}{свинья (svinyá)}]{\ru{свинья} (svinyá) — a pig}

\label{lesson:RU-C60-pig}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Russian for a horse, then the Russian for a cow.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{свинья}}
\textbf{\ru{свинья}} (\emph{svinyá}) — \textquotedblleft{}a pig\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{свинья}} $\leftarrow$ Proto-Slavic \emph{*svinĭja} — inherited, built on the PIE word \emph{*suH-}, \textquotedblleft{}pig\textquotedblright{}, that gave Latin \emph{sūs} and English \emph{sow}; English \emph{swine} is a close cousin of the Slavic form. Vasmer thinks the root most likely imitates a pig's grunt \emph{su-}.
\end{cousinweb}
